links.comparator_used: Manual grading of retinal photographs by trained mid-level personnel at the primary care hospital, with positives referred or sent to a visiting general ophthalmologist. This was a non-randomized, alternate-week comparison, and AI results were over-read remotely by a retinal specialist.
links.outcome: Referral positives identified at point of screening, true positives, and referral adherence
links.effect: Referral positives 201/645 (31.2%) with AI vs 175/730 (24.0%) with manual grading, P=0.003. True positives 129/201 (64.2%) vs 11/116 (9.5%), P<0.001. Referral adherence for true positives 115/129 (89.1%) vs 17/22 (77.3%), P=0.158, not significant. AI false negatives were 5/444 (1.1%). Manual false negatives could not be assessed.
links.tradeoff: About 35% of AI referrals were judged unnecessary by the over-reader (72 false positives). Median screening time was longer with AI (6:30 vs 5:38 min) because of image upload. AI false negatives included 3 severe NPDR cases and 1 cataract case. The authors say the two modalities had different workflows, no adjudicated gold standard, and no randomization, so results are trends only.
links.quote: To observe the trends of the two screening modalities (Table 2 ), the proportions of patients with referral positive and TP were found to be significantly higher in the AI group.

design_hint: remote specialist over-reading of AI grading and referral tracking
